newsitem.title: USA: US High Court term marked by conservative rulings.
newsitem.headline: US High Court term marked by conservative rulings.

text.p: The Supreme Court term just ended will go down as a watershed, underscoring a conservative shift with landmark rulings limiting the power of Congress, lowering church-state separation and supporting free speech.

Although often split between five conservative justices and the four more liberal justices, the high court nonetheless unanimously agreed on the session's two of the most important cases -- rejecting doctor-assisted suicides and allowing a sitting president to be sued.
Legal experts said the 1996-97 term, which ended Friday, also reaffirmed the court's central role in a wide range of contentious issues affecting American political life.

"This is a delayed vindication of President Reagan's efforts (in the 1980s) to change the Supreme Court. It is ironic that it happens during the watch of President Clinton," legal expert Bruce Fein said.
He characterised the court term as one of the strongest for conservatives in years.
Georgetown University law professor Paul Rothstein said the term saw the sharper emergence of the conservative and liberal factions.

On the court's right wing are Chief Justice William Rehnquist, who was elevated to his current post by Reagan in 1986, and Justices Antonin Scalia and Clarence Thomas, named by Republicans Reagan and President George Bush, respectively.
They often are joined by the moderate conservatives, Justices Sandra Day O'Connor and Anthony Kennedy, both named to the bench by Reagan.

The court's liberal wing consisted of Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer, both Clinton appointees; Justice David Souter, a Bush nominee, and Justice John Paul Stevens, named by Republican President Gerald Ford in 1975.

"It also became clear -- it had been intimated earlier -- that they are rewriting certain areas of constitutional law," Rothstein said. "They are rewriting the constitutional jurisprudence that had been spawned by a more liberal group of justices."
On free-speech, the Supreme Court for the first time declared that the Internet computer network deserved full constitutional free-speech protection from government regulation or censorship.
The justices refused to create a new constitutional right for Americans to commit suicide with the help of a physician, leaving the issue up to the states to decide.

The high court also said Congress exceeded its power by forcing local sheriffs to conduct background checks of prospective handgun buyers and by giving greater protection to the exercise of religious rights from government regulation.

And the court lowered the wall of separation between church and state, overturning a decision from 12 years ago and allowing public school teachers to go into parochial schools to offer certain remedial help.
"After several years of feeling its way, the court's personality is now clearly emerging," said Steven Shapiro, the American Civil Liberties Union's national legal director.
"This is a court that generally supports free speech. It also believes in state's rights. And it is more sceptical of federal authority than any court in recent history," he said.
"It is, in addition, a court that believes in neutrality more than it believes in equality. That is especially true in race cases," he said.
Clinton in the past month suffered a pair of stunning defeats at the high court.

The justices first said Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against Clinton may proceed rather than wait until he leaves office, rejecting his argument that facing such civil lawsuits would prove too distracting and a burden.

The court handed another setback to Clinton, requiring that the White House turn over to Whitewater prosecutors notes taken by its lawyers with first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton about her role in the affair.
During the term, the court handed down 80 opinions, up slightly from last year. Attorney Tom Goldstein, in a statistical analysis, calculated that 18 of the decisions were decided by a 5-4 vote.
The court, with no change in its makeup expected, will reconvene next in October after its regular summer recess.
